title: Bidirectional BFS in Chicago: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch two simultaneous BFS searches expand from start and goal across Chicago’s street grid—then stop the moment they meet. This “meeting in the middle” strategy shrinks the explored area and speeds up shortest-path discovery.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — How launching two searches doubles graph traversal speed ⚡

In this Chicago (Loop) route viz, you’ll see BFS run from:
1) the start node (forward frontier)
2) the destination node (backward frontier)

Each step expands the frontier level-by-level, but instead of exploring outward from only one side, we *converge*. The moment a node appears in both visited sets, we’ve found a shortest path—and we avoid wasting work in the “far” regions.

Key mechanics (the coding interview essentials):
- Maintain two queues: qF and qB
- Maintain two visited maps/sets (optionally with parent pointers to reconstruct the path)
- Always expand one frontier by one BFS layer (optionally choose the smaller frontier for extra speed)
- Stop when visitedF ∩ visitedB ≠ ∅

Takeaway: Bidirectional BFS keeps the shortest-path guarantee while reducing explored states from roughly O(b^d) to about O(b^(d/2)) in many graphs.

Debate question: In your experience—does Bidirectional BFS feel “worth it” only on large graphs, or can it outperform standard BFS even on smaller ones?
